title: Volume
caption:
Price tells you what happened. Volume tells you how much conviction was behind it.

A breakout on rising volume means lots of traders agree on the move. A move on thin volume is easier to reverse. And a sudden spike often marks news, or a turning point.

On Meme Street, volume swells on breakouts and fades in quiet ranges, just like a real market.

title: Support Resistance
caption:
Why does price keep stopping at the same spot?

Support is where buyers have stepped in before. Resistance is where sellers have. The more a level is tested, the more traders watch it.

When resistance breaks, it often becomes support. But levels are zones, not exact lines, so a stop goes beyond the level, not right on it.

title: Macd
caption:
MACD looks complicated. It's really just two moving averages talking to each other.

It's the gap between a fast and a slow average. The signal line smooths it out: crossing above means momentum is turning up, below means it's turning down. Shrinking histogram bars mean momentum is fading.

Like any average, it lags, and it chops in sideways markets.

title: Bollinger Bands
caption:
When these bands squeeze tight, pay attention.

Bollinger Bands are a 20-period average with a band two standard deviations either side. When the market goes quiet, they squeeze, and a squeeze often comes before a bigger move. It just won't tell you which way.

And touching the upper band isn't a sell signal on its own. Strong trends can ride it for a long time.

Why do so many traders care about 61.8%?

title: Atr
caption:
Your stop keeps getting hit by normal noise?

ATR, the average true range, measures how far price typically moves in one candle. Low when the market's calm, high when it's wild. It says nothing about direction, only size.

Many traders use it to size stops, for example two ATRs from the entry, so ordinary noise doesn't knock them out.

title: Candlesticks

Every chart is made of these. Here's how to read one.

Together, they tell a story. A long upper wick means buyers pushed up, and sellers pushed it back.

title: Position Sizing
caption:
How much should you put in one trade? Here's the simple maths.

Say you have 1,000 MB and risk 1% per trade: 10 MB. If your stop is 5% away, your position is 200 MB, because 5% of 200 is 10.

That way, even ten losses in a row leave you with about 90% of your account. No single trade can sink you.

title: Risk Reward
caption:
You can be wrong most of the time and still not lose money. Here's how.

Compare what you risk with what you aim to make. Risking 1 to make 3 is very different from risking 1 to make 1. At 1 to 3, you can be wrong three times out of four and still roughly break even.

But the target has to be realistic, like the next resistance level.

title: Gaps
caption:
Why do charts sometimes jump, with nothing in between?

That's a gap: price opened far from the last close, often because of news or earnings. Some gap and go, running on strong volume. Others fade back and fill the gap. Volume after the gap is often the best clue.

Meme Street has earnings every couple of days. Practise at memestreet.net

title: Oil
caption:
One price that moves almost everything else.

Oil is one of five commodities on Meme Street. In the real world it powers transport, flights and plastics, so when oil moves, costs ripple through the whole economy. Supply shocks can move it fast.

What can push it down: a slowing economy, extra supply, and inflation data that changes the outlook.

title: Too Much Leverage
caption:
At 10x leverage, a 10% drop can wipe you out.

Leverage multiplies everything. Without it, a 10% drop costs 10%. At 2x, it costs 20%. At 10x, it can cost everything you put in.

Learn it with practice money first. Pro players on Meme Street can use up to 10x, so you can see exactly what it does before it matters.

title: Flags
caption:
A sharp rally, then a quiet pause. Here's what it might mean.

A bull flag starts with a sharp rally, the pole, then a quiet drift lower on light volume, the flag. When price breaks out of the flag, the trend often continues.

Flags fail too: watch out if it drifts too deep or the pullback has heavy volume. A stop below the flag limits the damage.

title: Copper
caption:
Why do traders call it Doctor Copper?

Copper is one of five commodities on Meme Street. In the real world it's in almost every electric cable, plus buildings and electric cars. Because it's used everywhere, its price is seen as a health check for the economy.

What can push it down: a slowing economy, new mines and weak building data.

title: Leveraged Funds
caption:
Twice the move. And twice the risk.

Meme Street has 2x and 3x long funds, plus short funds that aim to rise when prices fall. They're mostly used for short-term trades.

Losses multiply just like gains. In real markets, funds like these usually reset daily, so holding them for a long time can drift from the target, especially when markets chop.
